extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of hydrostatics, experimental physicists, and mathematicians interested in fluid mechanics
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted operational laws and experimental guidance for hydrostatics: how lateral pressure depends on height, how to measure it experimentally (balances, placement), how air interacts with water pressure, and how syphons and fountains operate (force as difference of columns).

rubrics_metrics.name: The Lateral Pressure adapts itself to the Height, and not to the Breadth of Water
rubrics_metrics.description: (Original wording) 'The Lateral Preſſure adapts itſelf to the Height, and not to the Breadth of Water.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation and experimental verification: changing the breadth (by inserting a partition) while keeping the same height does not lessen lateral pressure; augmenting or lessening the height accordingly augments or lessens the lateral pressures. Example experiment: place a flat board so the breadth is halved but the water height unchanged; lateral pressure remains the same.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place the pressing part of the balance exactly at the centre of pressure
rubrics_metrics.description: (Original wording) 'It is to be obſerv'd, that the preſſing Part A of the Ballance AEF, muſt be placed exactly upon the Point of the Wood A, where the Center is, or where the lateral Preſſure is ſtrongeſt.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experimental guidance: use a cross piece to raise/lower the balance axis until the pressing arm contacts the exact point A. If the balance presses higher or lower than A the board yields under a much smaller weight, demonstrating the true point of strongest lateral pressure is at A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lateral pressure at a point equals weight of a vertical column whose height equals the depth at that point
rubrics_metrics.description: Implicit from multiple calculations: the lateral pressure on a plane at a given depth corresponds to the weight of a column of fluid of that height (used repeatedly in computations and experimental comparisons).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to compute resisting forces (e.g., converting 'a foot of water' into a pound weight); experiments compare measured resistance with computed column weights to verify hydrostatic rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surrounding air alters but scarcely changes water's lateral pressure
rubrics_metrics.description: (Original wording) the surrounding air 'does only leſſen the lateral Preſſure of the Water = part; which in the foregoing Experi­ment can make no ſenſible Alteration, and conſequently the aboveſaid Difficulty is obviated.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calculation method: include the weight of the air column acting on surfaces, but because water is ~1000× heavier than air the effect is often negligible for practical experiments; nevertheless account for it when precision requires.

rubrics_metrics.name: When computing pressures, include both water and air column contributions at each horizontal plane
rubrics_metrics.description: Throughout syphon and fountain analyses the pressure on an element is taken as the sum (or difference) of weights of the overlying water-column(s) and the incidant air-column(s) acting on the same horizontal plane.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: treat air-columns as c, water-columns as b, etc., and compute downward and upward forces by adding corresponding column weights; the net force on an orifice is the difference between these sums.

rubrics_metrics.name: Syphon force = difference of weights of the connected columns (water minus air)
rubrics_metrics.description: (Original wording/paraphrase) 'This ſhows the Force wherewith I K is preſs'd downwards more than upwards, and it is equal to the Weight by which the Water-Column RQKI ... exceeds the Air-Column PSTV ... So that ... the Water at the Orifice of the Tube IK, is by the lately mention'd difference of Weight between the two Columns PQKI and RS TV ... preſs'd or protruded downward to Z.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational criterion: the syphon will flow as long as the driving (longer) water-column weight exceeds the opposing (shorter) water/air combination; compute net driving force as b − c (water column less equivalent air column).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fountain stream height determined by effective sum of driving water columns minus air columns
rubrics_metrics.description: (Paraphrase of the fountain calculations) the water is propelled from the nozzle with a force equal to the weight of the pertinent water-columns (e.g., 2R and YZ) minus the weight of the corresponding air-columns (T3 and 4M).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conclusion drawn: the stream may rise higher than the water-supply level because the effective driving head equals the combined heights of the contributing water columns when air contributions are small and apparatus is arranged to transfer pressures via communicating vessels and trapped air.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion produced by removing a resistance equals the difference of the previously balanced pressures
rubrics_metrics.description: (Original wording/paraphrase) 'Motion may likewiſe be produced, by removing a Reſiſtance which obſtructed Motion... this Reſiſtance or Finger being taken away, a Motion will be made towards the Side of the Reſiſtance; and even with that Force with which the Reſiſtance was preſs'd when the Fluids were quieſcent.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experimental method: create a balanced (stagnant) state with an impediment (finger, cock); on removal the fluid moves toward the side previously opposed by the impediment, with force equal to the prior pressure difference, unless other forces immediately arise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fluids in communicating vessels have equal pressures at the same horizontal level regardless of tube shape or breadth
rubrics_metrics.description: (Implied by examples and the 'thread' thought-experiment) parts of the same horizontal plane that can be joined by a 'thread' without crossing other fluid or solids have equal upward and downward pressures when quiescent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to simplify calculations by equating forces on equal-area elements across connected regions; central to reasoning about syphons, fountains, and curve-tube experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hydrostatic paradox: base pressure depends on height, not total volume or breadth
rubrics_metrics.description: (Original phrasing paraphrase) in the multiple-tube example: although the water in each separate tube presses on the base with 100 pounds, opening all three does not produce triple the pressure — the pressure on the base is determined by the height, not by the total amount of water above.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experimental warning and conceptual point: do not infer base load from apparent 'sum of column weights' of separate branches; compute pressure from the relevant column heights at the base (this resolves the seeming paradox).

rubrics_metrics.name: When calculating forces in experiments, one may partition horizontal planes into equal parts and sum corresponding column weights
rubrics_metrics.description: Used repeatedly: divide a horizontal plane into equal parts (LM, NO, PQ, RS) and assign weights a, b, c to air or water columns above them, then compute net forces by adding/subtracting those column weights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This decomposition is an accepted bookkeeping device in the text for turning continuous pressure distributions into discrete computations; the author cautions the numerals (100,10,1) are illustrative, not literal physical ratios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curve-tube phenomenon: net motion determined by water column weight exceeding equal-height air column
rubrics_metrics.description: (Original example) in the curve-tube experiment, after removing the finger, the part F is pressed downwards because the little water-column AF (b) exceeds the equal air-column GE (c), so AF sub-sides until AF becomes air and equilibrium is restored.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prediction rule: when a trapped water column sits under an inverted glass over one leg, the column will fall/subside as long as the water-column weight exceeds the equivalent air-column weight; compute net force as b − c.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apparatus and measurement practice: balances with rectangular arms and adjustable axis to locate point of strongest lateral pressure
rubrics_metrics.description: (From experimental descriptions) use a balance AEF with arms rectangular at E, suspend weights at Y; make the pressing part adjustable by means of a cross-piece so the axis E can be thrust up or down to find the true centre of pressure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical tips: ensure pressing part contacts the true centre (A) of the test plate; if contact is off the required resisting weight will be smaller. Use thin cocks or stop-cocks, snug emplastring at joints, and consider thickness of cock when comparing upward/downward pressures at a plane.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use approximative numerical symbols for didactic computations but note they are schematic, not precise
rubrics_metrics.description: (Original note) 'we do by no means pretend that theſe Numbers of 100, 1, 10, &c. are the juſt Proportions of the Weight of Water and Air; but that we only mear there­by, to ſhow that a Column of Water is much heavier than a like Column of Air...'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pedagogical guidance: employ round illustrative numbers to make reasoning accessible to readers unfamiliar with symbolic calculus, but do not mistake these placeholders for measured physical constants.
